item.title: September’s Two Observances Are Counting the Same People
item.description:
Suicide

September’s Two Observances Are Counting the Same People

Research suggests thousands of suicides are recorded as accidental overdoses.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • As many as 30% of overdose deaths ruled accidental/undetermined may be suicides, according to a new analysis.
  • People with alcohol, drug, and tobacco use disorders have about 11 times the odds of dying by suicide.
  • Clinicians should ask about suicidal intent after every nonfatal overdose and throughout addiction treatment.
Source: Kampus Production / Pexels.com

Recovery Month and Suicide Prevention Awareness Month both fall in September. One focuses on people who struggle with addiction, and the other focuses on people we have lost to suicide and those still at risk. In most communities, they run on parallel tracks. The recovery rally and the suicide prevention walk rarely share a stage, and the people planning them don’t often sit in the same meetings.

I have worked with grief, trauma, and addiction for more than 35 years, and I’ve long suspected the two observances are talking about a lot of the same people. This summer, a group of researchers put some solid numbers behind that hunch.

What the Death Certificates Miss

In a commentary published online in July in Injury Prevention, injury epidemiologist Ian Rockett, psychiatrist Eric Caine, and their colleagues looked at U.S. deaths from 2000 through 2024. Over those years, the suicide rate rose 37.5 percent and drug poisoning deaths more than tripled. Yet the rate of drug poisoning deaths officially recorded as suicide went from only 1.3 to 1.8 per 100,000.

If overdose deaths tripled and suicides climbed by more than a third, you would expect overdose suicides to rise along with them. Rockett estimates that as many as 30 percent of overdose deaths labeled accidental or undetermined could be suicides. Part of the problem is how intent gets decided. A medical examiner or coroner has to make that call after the person has died, and when there is no note and no documented psychiatric history, the ruling usually lands on accident. Rockett put it plainly: “Most drug overdoses are the result of motivated behaviors and aren’t ‘accidents’ in the strict sense.”

To get a sense of scale, take the CDC’s latest provisional count of 67,798 overdose deaths for the 12 months ending in March 2026. The official suicide total for 2024 was 48,824. If one in ten of those overdoses was really a suicide, the national suicide count would be roughly 14 percent higher than what we report, and that uses a figure well below Rockett’s estimate. Those deaths aren’t counted as suicides when agencies decide where suicide prevention dollars and research should go.

What Survivors Tell Us

Studies of people who survive an overdose point the same way. In 2019, Hilary Connery and her team at McLean Hospital surveyed 120 adults in treatment for opioid use disorder about what they were feeling right before their most recent overdose. Just over half (58.5 percent) said they had at least some desire to die, and about 21 percent said they definitely wanted to die.

None of that surprises me. When I have asked clients about an overdose, what they’ve told me rarely fits the categories on a death certificate. I hear about exhaustion and about not caring about whether they woke up. Some used more than usual on the anniversary of a death, after losing a custody hearing, or on their first night home from jail. Intent runs along a continuum, and a lot of overdoses fall somewhere in the middle.

The link holds when you start from the other end. Lynch and colleagues (2020) compared people who died by suicide with matched controls across eight U.S. health systems. Those with alcohol, drug, and tobacco use disorders combined had about 11 times the odds of suicide death after adjusting for other risk factors. Among women with multiple substance use disorders, the odds were nearly 17 times higher.

How Big the Overlap Is

SAMHSA released its 2025 National Survey on Drug Use and Health in July. An estimated 44.6 million Americans age 12 and older had a substance use disorder in the past year. Among adults, 13.9 million had serious thoughts of suicide, 4.9 million made a plan, and 2.3 million attempted suicide. About 18.5 million adults had both a mental illness and a substance use disorder.

I think the treatment gap is the most concerning to me. Only 16 percent of people with a substance use disorder got any substance use treatment last year, which leaves roughly 38.5 million people who received no treatment or services at all. Many of them are at high risk for suicide and will never be asked about it by a clinician.

There are real reasons for hope in the numbers, too. Overdose deaths are down about 12 percent from a year earlier, and 73 percent of adults who report having had a substance use problem consider themselves in recovery. Most people do get better, and Recovery Month is a good time to remind people of that.

When Risk Is Highest

Risk tends to spike during transitions. After someone leaves detox, residential treatment, or incarceration, their tolerance is lower, and their stress is usually much higher. Binswanger and colleagues (2007) followed people released from Washington State prisons and found their risk of overdose death in the first two weeks out was about 129 times that of the general population. Those are also the weeks when people get turned down for jobs and housing, find out which relationships survived, and carry a lot of shame, all known drivers of suicidal thinking.

A return to use after time in recovery is another dangerous point. Clients often tell me a relapse proves they’ve failed, and that belief can slide into hopelessness fast. Put hopelessness together with lower tolerance and a drug supply nobody can predict, and it becomes very hard to say where an accidental overdose ends and a suicide attempt begins.

What Would Help

Emergency departments, recovery programs, and outpatient clinics that see someone after a nonfatal overdose should consider the possibility of suicidal intent and ask about intent directly, ideally with a validated screening tool. It takes a minute or two, and in my experience, people answer honestly when the question comes from someone who seems to care about the answer.

Suicide screening also belongs at every stage of addiction treatment, including intake, discharge, and after any return to use. For this population, a good safety plan includes naloxone, a conversation about access to firearms and other lethal means, and the name of a specific person to call.

On the data side, Rockett and Caine recommend a measure called self-injury mortality, which counts recorded suicides together with most deaths from drug self-intoxication. It sidesteps the problem of guessing intent after death and gives policymakers a more accurate read on how many people we are actually losing. Better training and more consistent standards for medical examiners and coroners would help as well.

Locally, the two September campaigns could simply start working together. Recovery organizations can include suicide prevention in their events, and suicide prevention coalitions can invite people in recovery to speak. Plenty of people also don’t know that the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline takes calls about substance use.

A Question From My Own Practice

One of the questions I’ve relied on most in my practice is some version of, “What has kept you going this far?” In solution-focused therapy, we call this a coping question. I’ve used it with people in early recovery and with people who are thinking about ending their lives, and it tends to land with both because it turns their attention toward the ways they have already managed to survive.

The two September observances will probably keep their own logos and events, but I would like to see the people who work in each of them start asking the other’s questions. A counselor in a recovery program can ask about suicidal thoughts, and a crisis line worker can ask about drinking and drug use. Neither question takes long to ask.

If you or someone you love is contemplating suicide, seek help immediately. For help 24/7 dial 988 for the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline, or reach out to the Crisis Text Line by texting TALK to 741741. To find a therapist near you, visit the Psychology Today Therapy Directory.

item.title: What Do We Understand About Blame?
item.description:
Guilt

What Do We Understand About Blame?

To err is human and to blame also seems to be human.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Blame is something that can help us and hurt us.
  • We use blame to regulate our feelings and to seek justice in the face of harm.
  • Too often the causes of anxiety, depression, or self-harm are fueled by self-blame.
  • Self-care in the face of self-blame is found in seeking help to untangle the suffering that you don't deserve.

We blame nature, we blame God, and we blame our enemies, spouses, and ourselves. We even blame politicians for never taking the blame!

What Is Blame?

Blame means to hold responsible, to find fault with, or to censure someone or something that has happened, has failed to happen, or has had a negative impact in some way.

The Purpose of Blame

We use blame for the regulation of feelings, the reparation of harm, and the restoration of order on personal, interpersonal, and broadly social levels.

In the best of circumstances, blame for wrongdoing, once acknowledged, results in apology, concessions to meet the demands of restorative justice, or punishment to meet the demands of retributive justice.

  • With Toyota's commercial truck company's agreement to pay 1.6 million for faking emissions tests, we see evidence of justice resulting from blame.
  • When a partner takes on the blame for their infidelity as the cause of heartache and disruption in a marriage, they restore trust, show love, and perhaps the possibility of reconnection.

The Misuses of Blame

Blame is complex and, like most human dynamics, rarely unfolds smoothly. The inability to blame, the projection of blame on others, and retaliation for blame with an imposed code of silence in the face of mistreatment are all misuses of blame that are incompatible with regulation, restoration, and recovery.

When a 12-year-old teen runs from sexual abuse in the home to the hands of a pimp, she rarely knows why the courts see her as “the one to blame.”

When people finally stand up in revolt against the oppression of a monarch, and the response is blame for civil unrest and retaliatory attacks on them and their children, we see another misuse of blame.

The Danger of Self-Blame

Although self-blame may be warranted as personal acknowledgment and rectification of actual wrongdoing, we often use self-blame when we are innocent of any wrongdoing. It is often an attempt to regulate unbearable feelings or situations that are out of our control.

In her book, Trauma Bonding and Interpersonal Crimes, Joan Reid (2024) discusses the emotional attachment victims develop toward their abusers, whom they defend as their only predictable attachments. Similarly, a child will often blame themselves to cover parental abuse.

In a contribution to our understanding of the formation, intensity, and persistence of guilt in Holocaust survivors, psychoanalyst and survivor Alfred Garwood (1996) suggests that "survivor self-blame" had the initial and principal function of reducing the pain and anguish of intolerable powerlessness in the face of annihilation risk and overwhelming loss. The ultimate result was obstruction of the mourning process and suicidal despair.

In his powerful book, Where War Ends: A Combat Veteran’s 2,700-Mile Journey to Heal (2019), Tom Voss shares his self-blame and his experience of moral injury for inflicting and witnessing the wounds of war. Having the chance to speak with Tom personally, I learned that he found a way to heal by walking across the country and meeting other veterans, whose connection and stories relieved him of his self-blame.

Our Own Blame

In the trauma work I have done over many years, I have never met anyone who has suffered a natural or man-made disaster, or even a serious medical diagnosis, who did not, in some way, blame themself. It would seem that we would rather regulate our existential helplessness with blame than consider that we cannot control life’s assaults.

The Impact of Other’s Blame

Self-blame is often fueled by the need of others to blame the victim as a way to psychologically distance themselves — “She should never have taken the train so late.” “He never watched what he ate.” “They insisted on living abroad.”

The inevitable consequence of incurred self-blame is not only guilt but a sense of shame, which is reflected in a lack of confidence, self-disdain, and fear of exposure. Too often, it precludes the necessary empathy we need from ourselves to heal.

When blame is warranted and constructive, it can lead to actions that regulate us personally and interpersonally. The owning of blame is reparative and restorative to oneself and/or the recipient of wrongdoing, be it a neighbor, lover, or foreign country.

Source: Istock/Siarhel Khaletski

But blame should not come to define your life. If self-blame persists, it eventually becomes the only feeling allowed. At some point we need to mourn, to tolerate rage, to acknowledge fear, to accept our limitations, to self-forgive, to unlock ourselves from blame and embrace the path going forward.

"Start where you are. Use what you have. Do what you can." –Arthur Ashe

item.title: The Psychology of World Peace
item.description:
Psychology

The Psychology of World Peace

The science of cooperation suggests war is irrational. Peace is natural.

Posted September 22, 2026

Source: Bobby Azarian/ChatGPT

Yesterday was World Peace Day. I spent it thinking about a message my cousin sent me from Tehran earlier this year.

After President Trump warned Iran that if the Strait of Hormuz wasn't opened "you'll be living in hell," I wrote to her pleading for her family to leave the city. She's in her twenties. She wrote back:

"Tonight is a difficult night for us, pray for us, the sounds are really loud, I hope the war ends as soon as possible."

I have dozens of family members living in Tehran. And, to be honest, like most people I might not have felt the urgency I feel now if it weren't personal. We are wired to feel the suffering closest to us most acutely. That's not a moral failing. It's biology. But if we genuinely believe that every innocent life has equal value, then we have to reckon with an uncomfortable gap between what we believe in principle and how we actually behave. The people caught in any war zone are someone's family. They are human beings no different from the ones we would risk our lives to protect. The distance between "someone's family" and "the enemy" is not a geographical distance. It's a psychological one.

And psychology, it turns out, is where a key part of the solution lives.

War Is a Design Problem

Most of us have been raised with a quiet assumption that war is unavoidable — a necessary evil baked into human nature and the way civilizations work. This assumption is wrong, and the science is increasingly clear about why. War is not simply a human nature problem. It is a design problem.

My colleague at the Evo-Devo Universe Research Institute, Clément Vidal, recently published a paper introducing what he calls the planetary cooperation barrier — the systemic misalignment that prevents humanity from coordinating at the scale our existential challenges demand. Drawing on cybernetics, evolutionary theory, and game theory, Vidal makes a deceptively simple argument: The current international order is not failing because human beings are inherently selfish or violent. It is failing because the architecture is wrong.

We have a world full of institutions generating accurate warnings about existential threats — nuclear proliferation, AI risk, and ecological collapse. What we lack is a governance layer capable of acting on those warnings. The knowledge exists. The structure to use it doesn't.

The historical precedent is instructive. In 1787, thirteen American states that were effectively in trade wars with each other, disputing borders and competing for advantage, came together at the Constitutional Convention. They did not abolish their individual identities. They integrated into a higher-level system that constrained their behavior on matters of collective concern while preserving what made each of them distinct. That is the model. Not a world government. Not the erasure of national sovereignty. Unity without uniformity.

Evolutionary theory suggests we are now at exactly this kind of threshold. The same logic that took us from single cells to multicellular organisms, from individuals to societies, now points toward a higher level of coordination among nation-states. This isn't utopian. It is what complex systems naturally do when the pressure is sufficient and the conditions are right. The question is whether we can make the conditions right deliberately, before catastrophe makes them right for us.

The Pseudospecies Problem

To understand why the cooperation barrier is so hard to break, you have to understand something about how human minds were built.

One of the stranger facts about our species is that we are a single biological species that repeatedly behaves as though we are many. In his 2002 book The Emergence of Everything, the complexity theorist Harold Morowitz used the term pseudospecies (coined by Erik Erikson) to describe this tendency: Human cultures construct boundaries between groups where no biological boundary actually exists. Religion, nationality, ethnicity, and political ideology can bind millions of strangers into a cooperative group — but the same mechanism that creates an us inevitably creates a them.

This produces something resembling what ecologists call competitive exclusion. In nature, two species competing for exactly the same resources in exactly the same niche cannot indefinitely coexist. When human groups come to see the world as a zero-sum competition for territory, resources, security, or identity, they import this logic into their politics. Each group begins treating the other as a competing population whose gain must be its loss.

Here lies the central paradox of human civilization: The same cognitive machinery that made large-scale cooperation possible can also tear it apart. Shared worldviews are extraordinarily powerful coordination technologies. They give people common values, common stories, and enough trust to cooperate with strangers. But once those stories harden into mutually exclusive identities, the coordination mechanism becomes a conflict mechanism. The tribe becomes a pseudospecies.

That is when another human being stops looking like someone's daughter or father and starts looking like an abstraction: Iranian, American, Muslim, Jew, Palestinian, Israeli, or enemy.

This is why propaganda is so psychologically potent. It does not merely give people false information. At its most dangerous, it degrades the resolution at which we model other human beings. A person becomes a category. And categories are much easier to hate than people.

The Cooperation Principle

This is where psychology offers something that policy alone cannot.

In research I've been developing on what I call the Game Theory of Mind, I describe a cognitive switch between two fundamental modes of thinking. The first — call it Mind A — is fast, reactive, tribal, and threat-sensitive. When we feel attacked or endangered, this mode rapidly sorts the social world into allies and enemies. It evolved to keep us alive in environments where that sorting mattered enormously. In many contexts, it still does.

The second mode — Mind B — is more regulated, reflective, and meta-aware. It can step outside the immediate emotional frame, model another person's perspective, examine its own assumptions, and ask whether a conflict can be transformed into cooperation by aligning interests rather than escalating opposition.

The point is not that we can reason our way out of every conflict. Human beings are not going to think their way to world peace through pure logic. The point is something more modest and more powerful: We can become aware of the psychological machinery driving the conflict. We can notice the us-versus-them program while it is running. And that awareness — that small gap between impulse and action — is where the possibility of peace lives.

The Cooperation Principle in Practice

The cooperation principle does not mean eliminating competition. Competition is useful. It generates variation, innovation, and excellence. The trick is to nest competition inside cooperation — to find the level at which former rivals share a larger objective.

American states compete for businesses, talent, and political influence while participating in a larger cooperative structure that constrains their most destructive impulses. The same logic has to move up another level. Countries can compete economically, scientifically, and culturally while sharing one non-negotiable commitment: do not destroy the game board.

This is the premise of the Manhattan Peace Project, an initiative I announced yesterday at my Substack, "Road to Omega." The original Manhattan Project mobilized an extraordinary concentration of scientific talent around what seemed like an existential problem. It succeeded. The question Project Unity asks is simple: What if we did that for peace? What if we brought together scientists, systems theorists, psychologists, artists, musicians, technologists, and ordinary people around an equally ambitious problem — not how to win a war, but how to make war obsolete? Let's find out.

item.title: Why We Rush Through the Things We Wanted
item.description:
Anxiety

Why We Rush Through the Things We Wanted

Getting what we want can pull us into overthinking, urgency, and control.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • Positive experiences can still bring pressure, uncertainty, and discomfort.
  • A person may respond to discomfort by overworking, maximizing, or trying to create control.
  • Mental fitness includes learning to stay present with discomfort while continuing to participate in life.
Source: Cortez Vernon / Used with Permission

I am in the middle of a really exciting time of my life. I feel like I say some version of that a lot. There is usually something I am creating or looking forward to; I think that's simply how I like to live. Yet, the part of me that creates a big life also makes it difficult to sit in it long enough to appreciate it.

Right now, something I have worked towards for years is finally happening. People are showing up for me. Opportunities I hoped for are here. I feel proud of what I created, and connected to why I created it.

The problem is, I can feel myself racing through the whole thing. For the past few weeks, I've heard myself saying, “I’m overwhelmed” too many times to count.

My skin is breaking out. I am eating Oreos before bed. My mind is moving fast. My calendar looks ridiculously full. A part of me always thinks that once I get the thing I've been working towards, I'll be able to relax and breathe a little. Then, I get there and realize I am still myself, still have my same patterns, and I am on to the next thing.

I have spent years teaching about being present and building capacity to experience discomfort instead of immediately trying to get rid of it. Then, something I worked incredibly hard for was almost here, and I caught myself a million miles ahead of it, buried under everything I thought I needed to do next.

Good Things Can Bring Up a Lot

It’s very human to think that stress automatically means whatever is happening is bad or wrong. What I am noticing is that the good things also stir up feelings of stress for me.

I meet someone I really like, and I'm suddenly finding new imperfections and qualities to add to my “list.” My business grows, and suddenly I'm wondering how much more I want to take on.

Apparently, a good thing can also take a toll on us. For me, it means more decisions, more responsibilities, and more ways for my brain to start spinning.

Psychologist Alison Wood Brooks studied what happens when people feel anxious before things like public speaking and other high-arousal tasks. In several of her studies, people who framed things as excitement when feeling arousal instead of trying to calm down sometimes performed better. Sometimes that icky feeling can just mean I care a lot about what's happening.

Source: Tara Winstead / Pexels

What Do I Do When I Feel This Way?

My default response is usually action: Do more. Fit more in. Make sure I have not missed something.

I have two patterns that tend to travel together. I call one "go mode": big energy, big ideas, moving quickly toward something that sparked my attention and matters to me at the time. "Go mode" has helped me build things I am incredibly proud of. The problem is the speed I go to get there. The quickness creates anxiety. I also get so locked in and focused on the next thing that I can completely miss what is happening in front of me.

The other pattern is maximizing. In decision-making research, maximizing means continuing to look for the best possible option instead of accepting one that is good enough.

Researchers Oren, Dar, and Liberman found an association between obsessive-compulsive tendencies and greater maximizing. This resonates with part of my own experience with OCD.

One good option can become: Is there a better one? One opportunity becomes: There has to be more.

Some of what I am doing right now is "go mode." Some is maximizing. Some is probably just me overcommitting and needing to say no.

I can spend forever naming the pattern. The win for me is noticing what I do once I am in it. Am I actually participating in what is happening, or have I become so busy managing the experience that I am no longer there?

The Goal Is Not Always to Feel Better

Psychological flexibility is our ability to notice what is happening inside of us, adjust when what we are doing is not helping, and move toward what aligns most with us.

For me, instead of "I need this to stop. How do I make this go away?" the practice is to stay long enough to see if it's part of what is important to me.

Sometimes, the discomfort is a sign that I am doing too much. My calendar can be too full. I may actually need sleep. Sometimes, the answer really is no. There is almost always one more email I could send, one more person I could call, one more idea I could execute.

The hard part is tolerating that possibility and stopping anyway. This moment, just as it is, without adding or changing, could be good enough.

Source: Alina Skazka / Pexels

The Practice Is Staying

So much is happening right now that I do not want to miss.

When I slow down enough and take a breath, I can feel and know that the work I am doing feels connected to my purpose.

I am proud and tired and excited, and yes, still uncomfortable. I have no idea what happens next.

My calendar did not magically clear because I recognized the pattern. I have not stopped having big energy or big ideas, and I do not want to. I am in the practice of noticing when doing more starts pulling me out of the moment I intended to be in. For now, this is perfectly enough.

item.title: The Most Creative Thing You Can Do Is Look Again
item.description:
Creativity

The Most Creative Thing You Can Do Is Look Again

Personal Perspective: System 2 thinking helps you spot hidden depth.

Posted September 22, 2026

Key points
  • True creativity comes not from chasing novelty, but from applying fresh curiosity to everyday routines.
  • Creative insights occur when shifting from automatic System 1 filtering to deliberate System 2 questioning.
  • Taking a second look reframed cheap plastic keepsakes into artifacts of human desire, identity, and memory.
Hernan Bas exhibition at Ca’ Pesaro
Source: Rod Judkins

I traveled to Venice hoping for fresh inspiration. When I returned, I realised I didn’t need to find something new. I just needed to view familiar things in a new way.

I visit Venice often. This summer, on my first day, I hurried past the tourists and rows of gaudy souvenir stalls stuffed with plastic trash. I was going to authentic Venice, the Ca’ Pesaro, International Gallery of Modern Art, to see the Hernan Bas exhibition.

I used to think portraiture was an old genre with nothing new to offer. Bas changed my mind. His paintings show tourists in front of the same cheap souvenirs I had just ignored. For Bas, plastic gondolas and flashy trinkets weren’t just clutter, they were important subjects.

He didn’t create a brand-new subject. Instead, he combined two things I thought were dull—portraiture and tourist souvenirs—and made me see them differently.

As I walked back through Venice, the souvenir stalls I once ignored now looked like small museums of what people want. They weren’t just things, they stood for identity, place, memory, and reminiscence. What I had avoided before, I now wanted to explore.

First Glance vs. Second Glance

Psychology helps explain how we see things. Our first look at the world isn’t neutral. Our brains are always sorting information, choosing what to notice and what to ignore. This helps us survive, since we couldn’t handle every detail all the time.

Psychologists call this System 1 and System 2 thinking. System 1 is quick and automatic. We judge things quickly, like seeing a souvenir stall and thinking it’s just cheap tourist stuff. We don’t have to look at every plastic gondola. This isn’t laziness; it’s our brain’s way of avoiding overload. But this speed can make us see things only on the surface.

System 2 thinking is slower and more thoughtful. It asks us to stop running on autopilot and really pay attention. Taking a second look is System 2 in action. We ask ourselves, "Wait, what am I really seeing?" That question can change everything.

At first, I saw the souvenir stalls as clutter to ignore. But Bas’ work made me reflect again; they became interesting examples of tourism, memory, and identity.

At first, I thought portraiture was an old, worn-out subject. Then I saw modern tourism as an intriguing mix of desire and myth. Creativity often starts between the first and second look.

Look Again

We often search for inspiration by traveling, going to conferences, and reading books about innovation. We want to find the next big idea, something no one else has seen. But sometimes, the most creative thing is to stop searching for something new and look again at what’s under your nose.

Take another look at the routine task you do every day. Think about the product everyone overlooks, the rule no one questions, the problem you’ve already decided can’t be solved, or the thing you once thought was boring, cheap, obvious, or unimportant.

The first look gives us an answer. The second look gives us a question. Creative thinking often starts when we get curious about that question.

Bas didn’t change the souvenir stalls; he made me see that I hadn’t really looked at them before. Maybe the best creative habit is not searching for something new, but learning to see what you already have in a new way.

Have you ever discovered something new by taking a second look at something you first ignored?
